description: Interactive geographic point map of 19 Australian National Surfing Reserves, coloured by state.

usermeta.title: Where are Australia's recognised surfing destinations?

All.callout: The Sydney-area cluster helps explain NSW's 11 of 19 listings (58%).
All.detail: 19 listed reserves · five states · dedication years 2006–2022
All.analysis: Australia's 19 National Surfing Reserves stretch across five states, from Kalbarri in Western Australia to Noosa in Queensland and Phillip Island in Victoria. New South Wales holds 11 listings (58%), with a pronounced concentration along the Sydney and wider NSW coastline. Yet the distribution also reveals markedly different coastal settings: WA's Indian Ocean-facing southwest, Queensland's subtropical point breaks and Victoria's exposed southern coast. These places represent different surfing communities and coastal identities, not a single uniform Australian surfing experience. The strong NSW cluster leads naturally to the next comparison: how much does each state contribute to the national register?

NSW.callout: Sydney contains five of NSW's 11 listed reserves.
NSW.detail: 11 reserves · 58% of national list · earliest 2006, latest 2022
NSW.analysis: New South Wales accounts for 11 of the 19 listings (58%), spread from Angourie and Lennox Head on the North Coast to Killalea in the Illawarra. Five lie in the Sydney region: Maroubra, Cronulla, North Narrabeen, Manly–Freshwater and Bondi. Maroubra became Australia's first National Surfing Reserve in March 2006, recognising a beach with established boardriding clubs and generations of surfing history. Merewether adds Newcastle's competitive surfing heritage to this east-coast network. Together, these sites reveal a particularly dense chain of recognised communities along the NSW coast, helping explain why NSW leads the state comparison in Chart 2.

QLD.callout: Gold Coast and Noosa form Queensland's two recognised coastal locations.
QLD.analysis: Queensland's two recognised reserves are the Gold Coast (2012) and Noosa (2015), both in the state's southeast. Although close together on the national map, they reflect different surfing identities: the Gold Coast designation includes renowned point-break areas from Burleigh Heads to Snapper–Kirra, while Noosa is known for its headland point breaks and longstanding longboarding community. Noosa has hosted its Festival of Surfing since 1998 and subsequently gained World Surfing Reserve status in 2021. These examples show how formally recognised sites can combine distinctive coastal geography, community heritage and major surfing events.

VIC.callout: Phillip Island is Victoria's one listed National Surfing Reserve.
VIC.analysis: Phillip Island, dedicated in March 2013, is Victoria's one entry in the national register. The designation encompasses several sections of its southern coastline, including Woolamai, Smiths Beach, Summerland and Cat Bay, where different reef and beach breaks respond to varying swell and wind conditions. The island's boardriding tradition stretches back decades, with its boardriders club founded in 1963. Although represented by one marker, the reserve itself embraces a network of coastal breaks; the map therefore highlights a broader Victorian surfing community through a single nationally recognised locality.

SA.callout: Point Sinclair and Daly Head lie on two separate South Australian peninsulas.
SA.detail: 2 reserves · Point Sinclair and Daly Head · both dedicated 2013
SA.analysis: South Australia's two listings, Daly Head on Yorke Peninsula and Point Sinclair on Eyre Peninsula, were both dedicated in January 2013. Their separation across two peninsulas highlights the geographic breadth of the state's recognised surfing heritage. Daly Head's history includes surfers camping and settling around the area's breaks from the 1970s onwards, eventually developing local boardriding clubs and a community-led nomination. The paired 2013 dedications illustrate recognition extending to longstanding surfing communities beyond Australia's densely populated eastern coastline.

WA.callout: Margaret River and Yallingup form a southwest coastal cluster.
WA.detail: 3 reserves · Margaret River and Kalbarri (2010) · Yallingup (2011)
WA.analysis: Western Australia's three recognised reserves occupy two distinct coastal regions: Kalbarri in the Mid West, and Margaret River and Yallingup in the southwest. Margaret River and Kalbarri were dedicated in 2010, followed by Yallingup in 2011. Margaret River's March 2010 dedication was especially significant as the first National Surfing Reserve in WA, extending the program across the continent. The southwest cluster reflects a region celebrated for varied reef breaks and a deeply established surfing culture, while the more distant Kalbarri listing shows that recognised heritage is not confined to the Capes.
